# A roadmap for integrating nutritional assessment, counseling, and support into the care of persons with tuberculosis

**Authors:** Pranay Sinha; Madhavi Bhargava; Madeline E. Carwile; Madolyn R. Dauphinais; Phumeza Tisile; Chelsie Cintron; Lindsey M. Locks; Janika Hauser; Matt Oliver; Scott Heysell; Saurabh Mehta; Julia L. Finkelstein; Kobto G. Koura; J. Peter Cegielski; Rein Houben; Finn McQuaid; Anurag Bhargava

## Abstract

Undernutrition, the leading risk factor for tuberculosis (TB) worldwide, is associated with impaired immunity, more extensive disease, delayed sputum conversion, and worse treatment outcomes, including mortality. This health policy piece proposes a comprehensive roadmap for integrating nutritional assessment, counseling, and support into TB treatment as part of person-centered care. At treatment initiation, we recommend standard nutritional assessment using anthropometric measurements and hemoglobin. We also recommend providing macronutrient and micronutrient support, alongside nutritional counseling, as indicated by the assessment.. Weight should be monitored during treatment, and lack of weight gain at the end of the intensive phase should prompt an investigation of causes, like food insecurity, poor treatment adherence, malabsorption, uncontrolled diabetes, or drug resistance. At the end of treatment, we recommend reassessing anthropometric measures to assess nutritional recovery. Persons with tuberculosis (PWTB) who remain underweight should receive close follow-up to detect early relapse. We call for annual reporting of nutritional metrics by the World Health Organization (WHO), explicit inclusion of nutritional assessment and care in national strategic plans, Global Fund support of nutritional programs for PWTB, increased support for operational research initiatives, and integration of nutritional care into the WHO Multisectoral Accountability Framework at national and regional levels.

## Introduction:

Approximately 1 in 4 human beings are latently infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), but progression to active disease is prevented in the majority of infections by cell-mediated immunity.1,2 Micronutrients and macronutrients play vital roles in immune system function, serving as co-factors for enzymes and substrates for the proliferation of immune cells and antibodies.3 Undernourished individuals have impaired cell-mediated immune responses to Mtb and exhibit a peripheral immune response profile marked by heightened inflammation, which may affect their risk of disease progression, disease severity, and treatment outcomes.2 Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection is associated with the highest risk of tuberculosis (TB), but nutritionally-acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (N-AIDS) is the most prevalent globally.1 Indeed, more TB cases worldwide are attributable to undernutrition than HIV infection because of the greater burden of undernutrition.1

The N-AIDS/TB syndemic is underpinned by a bidirectional biological relationship, with similar social determinants of health driving both undernutrition and TB.1 In addition, individual determinants such as age, alcoholism, parasitic infections, and HIV disease, and healthcare determinants such as diagnostic and therapeutic delays and inadequate primary health services drive undernutrition among PWTB and their household contacts (HHCs).4 Undernutrition blunts the immune response to TB, may reduce adherence, and may increase the risk of drug toxicity.1,2 In addition, undernourished individuals may have reduced respiratory capacity due to anemia and reduced respiratory muscular strength.5,6 These factors drive unfavorable outcomes such as death, treatment failure, loss to follow-up, and relapse.1 PWTB emerging from TB treatment with persistent undernutrition may have poor functional recovery. Additionally, N-AIDS increases risk of disease progression among HHCs. We have summarized this relationship in a conceptual framework. (Figure 1A)

Fortunately, undernutrition is a modifiable risk factor that can be identified and corrected through cost-effective interventions. Despite existing WHO guidelines, assessment of and care for N-AIDS are not yet standard elements of TB treatment.7 We provide a roadmap for implementing nutritional assessment, counseling, support, and monitoring in standard TB care. (Figure 1B)

## Treatment Initiation

### Assess and report baseline nutritional status.

Undernutrition in PWTB is most often a combination of pre-existing undernutrition and TB-related undernutrition. Current WHO guidelines recommend nutritional assessment at treatment initiation.7 Anthropometric measurements can provide vital prognostic information, as low body mass index (BMI) for adults or weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) for children can be readily collected by TB program personnel.1 Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is also an appealing, low-cost alternative, particularly in children and in pregnant adults, but the lack of universal cut-offs in adults may limit comparability across diverse regions.8 Studies from high-burden countries among adults and adolescents with both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB have consistently found low BMI and low MUAC to predict adverse outcomes and mortality.1,9,10 However, although weights are often measured for dose calculation, heights—needed for calculating BMI and WHZ—are often left unmeasured, leading to challenges in assessing nutritional status.

Unlike rates of HIV infection, which are uniformly reported in the WHO’s annual global tuberculosis report, there is no standard mechanism for reporting rates of undernutrition among PWTB.11 Instead, we are forced to rely on epidemiological studies that represent a few selected populations and restricted periods. Many studies do not report nutritional metrics at all. A systematic review identified only 57 studies from 1990–2022 that evaluated nutritional metrics among PWTB and reported a 48% prevalence of undernutrition.12 Systematic collection and reporting of BMI and WHZ data at treatment initiation for PWTB in annual TB reports would help us understand the scale of the problem, prioritize it, and strategize locally contextualized action on this modifiable risk factor. In the future, we need new tools that are scalable, cost-effective, validated against clinical outcomes, and able to address heterogeneity across populations and states of inflammation. What gets measured gets managed – not assessing nutritional status results in missed opportunities to address this modifiable comorbidity.11

### Evaluate and manage anemia

Anemia among PWTB is common, ranging from 30–94%, and multifactorial.13,14 At treatment initiation, most PWTB have anemia of inflammation, which should resolve with effective anti-TB treatment alone. However, nutritionally-driven anemia, particularly iron deficiency anemia, often co-exists with TB. Anemic PWTB have a nearly three-fold increased risk of mortality.13 Hemoglobin estimation should be a routine measurement in PWTB as it has prognostic value. Further, anemia can be severe enough to necessitate inpatient care and blood transfusion. Deworming may also be indicated in some settings.

Caution is warranted when it comes to managing iron deficiency. Iron is an obligate co-factor for mycobacterial enzymes that modulate metabolism and replication.15 As a result, mycobacteria have evolved intense iron-scavenging mechanisms. At treatment initiation, PWTB are likely to have elevated levels of hepcidin to limit mycobacterial growth. Hepcidin is a peptide hormone that controls the absorption of dietary iron by downregulating ferroportin, the protein responsible for iron transport into circulation, and release of iron from storage sites.16 Simply speaking, supraphysiologic iron supplements at treatment initiation are be less likely to be absorbed and may benefit the mycobacteria rather than the PWTB. Therefore, iron deficiency anemia should be addressed later during treatment.

### Provide nutritional support to persons with TB & household contacts.

The mortality risk due to TB disease is highest in the first two months of treatment.10 Highly relevant guinea pig models have demonstrated that repletion with protein-rich foods rapidly restores cellular immune responses to Mtb with resultant reductions in mortality.2 A similar effect is likely in humans as well. Therefore, prompt initiation of nutritional support after diagnosis is likely to be more effective than delayed provision of supplementation.

Although the 2013 WHO guidelines do not recommend specialized nutritional support for PWTB, they emphasize that severely underweight individuals, moderately underweight children, pregnant women, and those with drug-resistant TB should receive nutritional care consistent with general WHO recommendations.7 We recommend expanding this recommendation to persons with drug-susceptible TB who are moderately (BMI 16–17 kg/m2) or severely underweight (BMI < 16 kg/m2) since studies have shown an increased risk of mortality in these populations.10

Inexpensive food baskets to supplement the diets of PWTB, such as those provided in the RATIONS study (1200 Kcal/day, including 52g of protein), can meaningfully improve nutritional recovery and possibly treatment outcomes.17 Indeed, a cluster-randomized trial from Odisha recently showed that PWTB receiving standard therapy had an approximately 50–80% higher risk of unfavorable outcomes (death, loss-to-follow-up, and treatment failure) than those receiving food baskets.18 A recently conducted systematic review has also concluded that nutritional support improves treatment adherence.19

More research is necessary to determine the optimal composition of food baskets for PWTB and to tailor them to different populations, such as persons with severe undernutrition, persons with diabetes, children, pregnant women, or those having diets with a single dominant source of calories, such as rice or maize. Ultimately, the needs of PWTB depend on baseline food security and intake, and developing food baskets requires better understanding through mixed-methods studies. Food baskets must be concordant with the preferences and cultural context of each population. An excellent example is the food kit that the Kerala state government used to reduce food insecurity during the COVID-19-induced lockdowns. In addition to the dry rations, the kit also provided condiments, spices, and tea, which likely increased food utilization.20 Implementation research is necessary to determine the acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness of different delivery methods in different contexts.

For severely undernourished individuals, inpatient care may be necessary at treatment initiation to ensure adequate dietary intake and avoid refeeding syndrome. Differentiated care such as the Tamil Nadu-Kasanoi Erappila Thittam (TN-KET) in South India has begun triaging PWTB with BMI <14kg/m2 and those with BMI 14–16kg/m2 with edema to inpatient care, where they receive therapeutic milk supplementation for nutritional rehabilitation and are closely monitored as they initiate TB treatment.21

Cash transfers have also been used to improve food access among PWTB. A systematic review of cash transfers found that receiving cash transfers was associated with more than 75% improved odds of positive TB treatment outcomes.22 A recent analysis of 54.5 million recipients of Brazil’s Bolsa Familia Program found that conditional cash transfers were associated with an approximately 30% reduction in TB mortality and 40% reduction in TB incidence.23 It is plausible but unclear whether this benefit was through reductions in undernutrition. As a general principle, cash transfers work best for impoverished populations with access to functioning markets. And while studies have demonstrated improvement in food security among PWTB receiving cash transfers, there is no available evidence to demonstrate improvement in tangible nutritional metrics. This research gap must be addressed.

Although many existing nutritional subsidies focus on the nutritional needs of PWTB, economic shocks due to TB can affect all persons in a household, further increasing risks of TB incidence among HHCs. The RATIONS study provided empirical evidence that household-level nutritional support among impoverished households can reduce disease incidence among HHCs by approximately 40%.24 Moreover, models suggest that nutritional interventions for HHCs would be cost-effective.25 Nutritional interventions should be agnostic to the drug-resistance profiles and may have special relevance for undernourished HHCs of individuals with MDR-TB who are themselves at increased risk of incident drug-resistant TB.26 Indeed, nutritional support may have special relevance for those exposed to extensively drug-resistant (XDR)-TB or pre-XDR-TB as they currently lack pharmaceutical options for preventive therapy. Given these data, the quantity of food provided should support the entire household.

Nutritional support addresses multiple issues. It can be viewed first as therapy essential for undernourished PWTB, second as preventive therapy for household contacts, third as social protection against food insecurity and associated undernutrition in a milieu of TB-related economic distress, and finally, as an incentive for PWTB and their contacts to engage with care. Perhaps most importantly, when people impacted by TB in impoverished communities are asked how to improve outcomes, they frequently request nutritional support.1

### Provide nutritional counseling

Ensuring proper food utilization is also critical. Impoverished PWTB be at risk for nutrient deficiencies due to lower dietary diversity.1 While both in-kind and cash transfers may improve dietary diversity, nutritional misconceptions and traditional beliefs may lead to suboptimal utilization. When done effectively and in a culturally-competent way, counseling may be a vital enabler to enhance the utilization of in-kind or cash support for nutrition in PWTB. Counseling may improve the consumption of locally-available foods rich in micronutrients and address dietary misconceptions prevalent in the community.27 Nutritional counseling may also help manage the symptoms and side-effects of TB drugs such as nausea and vomiting, anorexia, diarrhea, and altered taste. Indeed, the WHO guidelines already recommend nutritional counseling for PWTB.7 However, nutritional counseling should not be added to the daily tasks of overworked TB program workers as they may not have the time or expertise to do it effectively. With training, compensation, and ready-to-use counseling guides, community health workers may be better suited for nutritional counseling.28

### Address reversible causes of undernutrition

Most of the weight loss among PWTB is caused the disease’s effects on metabolism and appetite, as well as food insecurity.1 Individuals may also have other reversible causes of undernutrition such as HIV and diabetes. Therefore, PWTB should undergo routine screening for these conditions. In tropical and sub-tropical regions with high prevalence rates of enteropathogens, testing and treatment may be warranted among undernourished PWTB.1 Depression, malabsorption, and alcohol use disorder are other reversible causes that may be at play in PWTB.4 As TB providers may lack the expertise and resources to care for several of these reversible causes, providers can screen and link PWTB for care as feasible in their context. Considering and addressing reversible causes of undernutrition for PWTB constitutes person-centered care.

## End of Intensive Phase

### Assess and report weight changes.

Weight gain is the prognostic biomarker we already have. Historically, reporting weight monthly was a standard part of the original International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease/World Health Organization “DOTS” system. TB clinicians know that return of appetite and weight gain, often within a couple of weeks of treatment initiation, reflects effective treatment, while stagnant weight may suggest the opposite. Indeed, lack of weight gain during TB treatment was associated with a five-fold increase in mortality and a 70% increase in unfavorable outcomes in a large Indian cohort.10 In this cohort, 60% of PWTB did not gain weight at the end of the intensive phase. Conversely, approximately 60% of PWTB enrolled in the RATIONS study gained 5% of their baseline body weight.17 Regaining 5% of their body weight was associated with an approximately 60% reduction in their mortality.

This threshold of 5% body weight gain at the end of the intensive phase has been associated with a decreased risk of relapse in other studies of both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB.1 More research is needed to validate this threshold, but it may be a good target for the end of the intensive phase, especially for PWTB who lost weight during treatment or who were undernourished at treatment initiation. Of course, weight gain may also necessitate adjusting doses of TB medications to ensure adequate pharmacokinetic exposure and avoid the emergence of drug resistance, particularly among children who do not gain weight.4 Given the prognostic importance and clinical implications of weight gain at the end of the intensive phase, measuring, recording, and reporting weight at the intensive phase should be a standard component of TB care.

### Assess & manage unresolved anemia

Inflammatory anemia responds to TB treatment, but anemia due to nutritional deficiencies does not.14 A study from Puducherry, India, found that 65% of PWTB who were anemic at baseline remained anemic despite completing TB treatment. Independent predictors of anemia include being underweight, poor socioeconomic status, and low iron intake based on dietary recall.29 Testing for persisting anemia at the end of the intensive phase can help identify individuals with nutritional anemias due to vitamin and mineral deficiencies, of which iron, folate, and B12 deficiencies are the most common.

The end of the intensive phase, particularly after sputum conversion, is likely a safer time to administer micronutrient supplements that include iron, as the mycobacterial load is lower. Moreover, hepcidin levels are also lower by the end of the intensive phase, making iron supplementation more effective.13,14 The role of malaria and intestinal parasitic infections must be considered based on the context. Biochemical assessments for B12 and folate and supplementation may be needed in individuals with normocytic or macrocytic anemia.14

### Address reasons for poor weight gain.

Beyond its role as a prognosticator, lack of weight gain at the end of the intensive phase should prompt investigation for an underlying cause. Several actionable factors, such as food insecurity, poor adherence to treatment, poor drug absorption, drug resistance, and comorbid conditions like untreated diabetes or HIV infection, can cause stagnant or decreasing weight despite intensive therapy. These factors can and must be remedied with specific actions such as enhanced treatment support with frequent check-ins with community health workers, drug susceptibility testing and correction of the drug regimen, therapeutic drug monitoring and dose adjustment, and provision of nutritional support and counseling. In essence, lack of weight gain is an inexpensive and accessible biomarker that can alert clinicians to insidious concerns and therefore must be assessed routinely in PWTB.

## End of Treatment

### Assess and report nutritional status.

Recording weight at the end of treatment may be a practical and inexpensive means of directly assessing the overall effect of treatment; microscopy and culture become negative long before the end of treatment, and abnormalities on chest imaging often do not resolve entirely by the end of treatment. Indeed, weight may be the only measurable metric among persons with extrapulmonary TB. Why, then, is measuring weight not routine? Again, we do not have clear metrics about nutritional recovery at the end of treatment and the quantity of weight gain that indicates treatment success. This gap can be remedied through systematic assessment and reporting.11 With robust data, we may be able to determine a target weight gain or BMI at the end of treatment to provide assurance of adequate treatment.

### Assess for relapse if undernourished

Lack of weight gain at the end of treatment should prompt an assessment for clinical failure and emerging resistance, just as it would at the end of the intensive phase. Nutritional status at the end of treatment is also a valuable prognosticator for relapse or recurrence.1 Indeed, PWTB who remain undernourished at the end of treatment may lack the immune response needed to clear remaining bacilli, resulting in early relapse. In high TB burden settings, PWTB may also be at increased risk of TB progression after a new infection.1 Therefore, PWTB who are undernourished at the end of treatment should receive radiographic and clinical evaluation 3–6 months after treatment completion to ensure early detection of relapse.

### Link to welfare and nutritional support schemes

Food insecurity post-TB treatment can perpetuate a vicious cycle of poverty, undernutrition, and disease. While national TB programs cannot be tasked with ongoing nutritional care for PWTB post-treatment, they can assist PWTB with navigating referrals to appropriate services. Many PWTB may be eligible for, but unaware of, nutritional support services and social welfare programs like healthy breakfast and lunch programs for children, take-home rations for pregnant and lactating women, transport concessions, and similar benefits. Linkages like these can ease food insecurity and improve person-centered outcomes.

National TB program personnel already have staggering clinical and administrative burdens. To avoid overwhelming them with additional responsibilities, they must be provided clear guidance about existing nutrition and social security schemes available in the country, and policymakers should also consider financial incentives. Technical innovations linking PWTB registered in national databases to available welfare programs could also ease administrative burdens for program personnel. Community health workers may also have an important role to play in post-TB nutritional care by conducting post-treatment nutritional assessment, monitoring, and support.28

## Conclusion:

The goal of TB diagnosis and treatment is not just to eliminate Mtb from the bodies of PWTB;. it is also to restore their health and their capabilities to care for themselves and their families. Prioritizing nutrition offers myriad positive externalities with beneficial effects on other infectious and non-infectious diseases, children’s physical and cognitive growth, and economic productivity, to cite a few.25 Nutrition is a cross-cutting issue, and addressing undernutrition among PWTB and those at risk for TB will help attain the UN’s universal healthcare goals and contribute to the attainment of sustainable development goal 2 (zero hunger). Integrating nutritional assessment, counseling, monitoring, and support throughout TB treatment is critical to provide holistic, person-centered care to PWTB. Some actions, such as nutritional assessment and prompt nutritional support for severely undernourished PWTB, should be prioritized immediately (Figure). Subsequently, integrating nutritional care for PWTB and TB survivors into broader health services, such as primary care and maternal health programs, could further enhance reach and impact.

Recognizing the importance of undernutrition as a barrier to TB elimination, the United Nations High-Level Meeting committed to multisectoral action on undernutrition. It is critical that this commitment is upheld, as most TB programs currently lack funding and specific expertise to manage undernutrition. The first tangible step that must be taken urgently is to start collecting and reporting national-level nutritional data for PWTB, which can be incorporated as a key TB metric in WHO annual reports. Further, specific nutritional objectives should be incorporated into national strategic plans, and funding for nutritional supplementation programs should be part of funding requests to the Global Fund. Concurrently, research agendas should prioritize undernutrition operational studies as they pertain to TB, along with training programs for public health scientists working on the N-AIDS/TB syndemic in the most affected regions.30 Lastly, nutritional assessment and care should be integrated into implementing the WHO Multisectoral Accountability Framework at national and regional levels.

It is time that we start seeing nutritional care not as an optional luxury but as a medical necessity—an intervention as fundamental as the medicines we prescribe. Feeding people is not just an act of compassion; it is a cornerstone of effective person-centered TB care.
